summary: A request for comments about the procedure for updating the naming registry and distributing host tables, as it exists and as it might. None of the proposals are standards.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 849 discusses how sites could keep local copies of the host table up to date. It suggests four update approaches and asks readers to comment on them.

questions: how did rfc 849 propose distributing host table updates
how could a site check its host table version
what host table update plan did the author prefer
subtitle: A request for comments on improving distribution of the Internet host table.

tldr.problem: Sites maintained local copies of HOSTS.TXT, but did not have a reliable automated way to learn when a newer version was available.
tldr.mechanism: The author discusses push updates, version checks, email distribution, and a combination of push with periodic polling.
tldr.outcome: The RFC asks for comments and says none of the proposed solutions is a standard at the time.

today: RFC 849 is a request for comments on host-table updating and distribution. It states that none of its proposed solutions are intended as standards at the time.

sections.title: The Host Table Update Problem
sections.content:
The memo says sites were expected to maintain local copies of the NIC's HOSTS.TXT file because the NIC was not reliable enough to act as a name server for every lookup.

A person at each site had to retrieve the latest file, and the RFC says updates were not always announced. It also notes the lack of a good automatic check for whether a local copy was current.
sections.plainLanguage: Sites needed their own copies of the host table, but could not easily tell when to update them. Downloading an unchanged file would waste effort.

sections.title: Four Update Approaches
sections.content:
The first suggestion is a protocol that lets the NIC send updates to registered hosts. The second is a version-check protocol so a site can find out whether its copy is current.

The third suggestion distributes the file by email, which the author considers problematic for large files. The fourth combines attempted push updates with polling at startup and periodically; the author says this combination seems best.
sections.plainLanguage: The ideas range from NIC-initiated updates to local version checks and email. The author's preferred option combines updates with a way for each site to check for missed changes.

sections.title: Longer-Term Name Service
sections.content:
The RFC also considers replacing or augmenting the NIC system with dedicated VAX Unix systems for a reliable, responsive name service. The author says this could eventually remove the need for local copies.

The memo describes that as a longer-term solution requiring money, time, and effort, and asks the community to comment on the shorter-term suggestions.
sections.plainLanguage: A more reliable name service could reduce the need for local copies, but the author says that approach needs more resources. This RFC invites discussion of both immediate and longer-term ideas.
